newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Boutros-Ghali in swan song tells U.S. to pay up.
newsitem.headline: Boutros-Ghali in swan song tells U.S. to pay up.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in a thinly veiled jab at the United States said on Tuesday the world body's financial crisis was caused by deadbeats and not by mismanagement.

"We know what causes it and what is needed to end it. It is not the result of mismanagement. It is the refusal to fulfil a treaty obligation," he said in his farewell address to the U.N. General Assembly before leaving office on Dec. 31.

"Now that a new secretary-general is being appointed, all arrears should be paid at once, as has been promised so often in the past few months," he said shortly before his successor, Kofi Annan of Ghana, was sworn in before the 185-member assembly. Boutros-Ghali received a standing ovation.

The Clinton administration blocked his bid for a second five-year term against the wishes of nearly all other U.N. members, saying he was sluggish in promoting reform. The 74-year-old former deputy prime minister of Egypt, law professor and author alienated the Republican-dominated U.S. Congress, which refused to pay $1.3 billion in U.N. arrears.

He said his five years in office were marked by "enthusiasm, disillusion and realism." Speaking in English, French and Arabic, he warned members that nothing was more precious to the United Nations than its impartiality, equity, efficiency, achievement and independence.

"If one word above all is to characterise the role of the secretary-general, it is independence," he said, in what could be interpreted as advice to Annan, the U.S.-educated head of peacekeeping, whose choice was supported by the United States.

"The holder of this office must never be seen as acting out of fear of, or in an attempt to curry favour with, one state or group of states," he said. "Should that happen, all prospects for the United Nations would be lost."
When he entered office in 1992, member states called on the United Nations to take action on an unprecedented scale: for peace, development, democratization and reform, he said.

In response, he launched his "Agenda for Peace" report that began an international debate on preventive diplomacy, peacekeeping and peacemaking, and the world body entered peacekeeping ventures from El Salvador to Cambodia, Angala and Mozambique.

But he said it was also clear to him the United Nations would have to undergo change and he simplified secretariat structures and began managerial reform. During the middle years of his term, however, disillusion set in, particularly when peacekeepers were asked to deal with warfare, as in Somalia, which weakened the will of the world community to act against genocide in Rwanda.
In Bosnia, too, he said, hard choices were avoided. "The concept of peacekeeping was turned on its head, and worsened by the serious gap between mandates and resources," he said.

On development, Boutros-Ghali said aid was declining and "Africa was hit hardest." And despite high hopes for democratization, human rights atrocities such as ethnic cleansing reached unprecedented levels.

He said it was also clear that extensive reform could only emerge from a political will among member states -- reform of the Security Council, the amounts each country would pay, the programmes the membership wanted to keep or abolish.

Nevertheless, Boutros-Ghali said that in the past year a new sense of maturity appeared possible, with a division of labour between the United Nations and regional organisations. Development was also being restored in a coordinated fashion.
"Most importantly," he said, "there is a new recognition that reform is not an end in itself."

"The test of true reform will be whether it will improve the capacity of the United Nations to meet those responsibilities and to advance the common objectives of the people of the United Nations and its member states," he said.
